---
title: "Data-driven archetypes of farmland change: Preliminary results"
author: Carolyn Koehn
abstract: |
  Approximately 1.5 million km$^2$ of global land was converted from agriculture to highly developed areas between 1992 and 2018. The processes leading to this conversion are variable, but most farmland protection policy focuses on controlling urban sprawl. A better understanding of the multiple contexts in which farmland loss occurs can inform the development of more diverse policies for agricultural land protection. We used an interdisciplinary archetypes approach that identifies recurring patterns of variables in social-ecological systems across different spaces and time periods. We combined finite Gaussian mixture model cluster analysis and qualitative case studies to find recurring patterns of change over time in 26 counties in southern Idaho's Snake River Plain, a region of the western United States [US] with both high agricultural production and high population growth where agricultural lands are at risk of conversion. We chose data linked to second-tier variables in the resource and actors subsystems in Ostrom’s social-ecological systems framework. Specifically, we calculated descriptive metrics for 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2020 from the US Census, land use/land cover spatial data, and the US Census of Agriculture. We found that these 26 counties over 4 time points clustered into 5 resource clusters and 4 actors clusters. Resource clusters were strongly driven by federal, forested, and shrublands and land near major roadways, whereas actor clusters were strongly driven by degree of urbanicity, average age, and number of hired agricultural workers. We then selected 4(?) counties from the full pool of counties to do qualitative case study analysis and link those insights with the results of the data driven clusters. Through combined quantitative and qualitative approaches, we found that agricultural land loss occurs in multiple contexts, including urban sprawl and in more rural areas with recreation access. We reveal spatially distant counties in the same archetype that may be able to share successful farmland protection policies, as well as neighboring counties in different archetypes that will likely require different policy pathways to protect farmland. We intentionally used publicly available data so that this approach could be applied to many areas grappling with agricultural land loss.

# Introduction

Approximately 1.5 million km$^2$ of land has been converted from agriculture to urban and highly developed areas between 1992 and 2018, amounting to 7.5% of total global land cover change in that 25-year period [@radwan2021]. The pathway to conversion is often attributed to urban or suburban sprawl [@chen2020; @vanvliet2017], and land use projections are based on the assumption that population growth will drive urban development of agricultural lands based on their proximity to an urban center [@xie2023; @chen2020; @haney2015]. However, there are other pathways to agricultural land conversion, such as housing development in rural settlements and increased construction of commodity processing and transportation facilities, that are rarely addressed alongside urban sprawl in land use change literature (for exceptions, see @ju2018 and @jiang2019). Even when other pathways to agricultural land loss impact a smaller land area compared to urban sprawl, they can have significant negative impacts on local ecology and crop production [@zhu2022] and social well-being [@smith2001]. In order to protect high quality agricultural lands, it is critical to understand the multiple pathways that those lands are converted to other uses. There are three recurring patterns of farmland loss that have been described separately in a number of case studies: urban/suburban sprawl, amenity migration, and agricultural industrialization.

Urban sprawl is a widely recognized pathway to agricultural land loss. As the population in urban centers grows, there is increased need for housing. While cities may create denser housing in the urban center to accommodate a larger population, they often expand outwards onto marginal lands as affluent, car-owning residents seek spacious suburban neighborhoods [@dieleman2004]. As suburbs encroach on agricultural land, farmland fragmentation makes farming more difficult and encourages further development [@latruffe2014; @qiu2015; @freedgood2020]. As near-urban farmlands rise in value, the number of senior producers far exceeds the number of young producers, and as demographic and culture changes make farming less appealing, the sale of agricultural lands to urban developers is an attractive offer [@kuethe2014; @freedgood2020; @sheridan2007]. High quality croplands are especially susceptible to urban sprawl as both farming and housing development are easiest on flat lands with more access to freshwater [@halperin2023; @bren2017]. Urban and suburban sprawl are a prominent cause of agricultural lands loss and are present in many land use change models focused on agricultural lands [@xie2023; @chen2020; @haney2015].

Industrial expansion is seen as a vehicle for economic growth and it has manifested diversely in different global regions. Across Asia, conversion of agricultural land to industry use precedes urban sprawl or occurs alongside urban sprawl [@azadi2011; @tuyen2013; @zhou2020]. In Europe, a large portion of manufacturing was shifted to rural areas in the late 1970s [@keeble1983]. In the United States, supply-oriented food manufacturing (e.g. cheese manufacturing) is likely to occur in rural agricultural areas with sufficient infrastructure and labor availability [@lambert2009]. Additionally, manufacturing facilities tend to agglomerate around certain urban or local economies so that the presence of one manufacturing facility is correlated with the presence of more [@lambert2009]. Besides conversion of agricultural land for manufacturing facilities, these factories attract non-local workers who will need housing, yet their settlement patterns may be different from those of urban migrants. For example, rural industrial restructuring is linked with Hispanic growth [@lichter2012]. Thus, the industrial expansion pathway to agricultural land loss manifests in a different manner than agricultural conversion due to urban sprawl. 

Amenity migration, the migration of affluent urban populations to rural areas for specific lifestyle amenities, is a pathway to rural land change, including agricultural land loss [@abrams2012]. Rural sprawl associated with amenity migration is less dense than urban sprawl, resulting in larger areas of land affected, but with less intensity [@radeloff2005]. Amenity migrants with agricultural estates do not rely on agricultural production as a means of income, and may engage in some form of farming (including hobby farms), lease lands to local producers, or use their lands for non-production uses like recreation and conservation [@abrams2012; @abrams2013]. Local jobs are primarily low-wage service jobs, and this combined with rising property values can push low income households farther out of the high-amenity community [@sherman2018; @loeffler2007; @abrams2012]. Thus, agricultural producers in high amenity communities may face rising costs and falling off-farm wages, the need to lease land, and the fragmentation of agricultural lands by migrant estates and commuter roads. Amenity migration is a distinct pathway to agricultural land loss that differs in cause and effects from urban sprawl and industrial expansion, and requires different policy and planning approaches to address.

Since agricultural land conversion occurs via different processes in different contexts, farmland loss may be best described by archetype analysis. Archetypes are recurring patterns of social-ecological variables that build towards middle-range theories -- generalizations that describe causal pathways within a well-bounded range of phenomena [@meyfroidt2018; @oberlack2019]. The three farmland loss pathways described above, urban/suburban sprawl, agricultural industrialization, and amenity migration, will require context-specific policies to control farmland conversion, and places with similar patterns of farmland loss may share successful policies. However, to our knowledge, multiple archetypes of farmland loss have not been identified in a generalized yet spatially and temporally explicit manner across a single study region. In the United States, long-term public datasets enable longitudinal studies of land use and demographic change that can construct dynamic archetypes, patterns of social-ecological variables that re-occur across both space and time. The intentional use of public data ensures that this analysis can be implemented across the country.

The Snake River Plain of Idaho is an ideal place to study multiple processes of farmland loss because it is experiencing different drivers of agricultural land conversion across its counties. We hypothesize that land use change is occurring due to urban/suburban sprawl, amenity migration, and agricultural industrialization in different areas across the region. This research will aid in identifying where distinct processes of land use change are occurring, contributing to a diverse toolbox for agricultural lands protection in diverse localities. We calculated descriptive metrics for 26 Idaho counties in 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2020 (104 units total) from the US Census, land use/land cover spatial data, and the US Census of Agriculture. Our research questions were:

1. Are there identifiable archetypes of social-ecological subsystems (resource and actors) in Idaho's Snake River Plain?
2. What are those archetypes, and which demographic, economic, and remotely sensed indicators are the most important characteristics of those archetypes?
3. What is the relationship between these archetypes and farmland loss?
4. Are there counties that have shifted archetypes through time, and what are their characteristics?

# Methods

## Data Selection

We linked data available from 1990-2020 to second-tier variables in Ostrom's social-ecological systems framework [@ostrom2009] based on expert knowledge from the authors. Some second-tier variables are excluded because no relevant data sources could be found. Detailed data sources and processing steps for each indicator and year can be found in Appendix A.

I scaled these data by mean normalization (divided by the range), so that all variables had a mean of 0 and range of [-1, 1]. In clustering, dividing by the range (scaling) is preferable to dividing by the standard deviation (normalization) to preserve possible cluster structure in the data [@hennig2016].

## Clustering - will be expanded in next draft

### Algorithmic Variable Selection

Before clustering begins, it is useful to select the most important variables for clustering. The `clustvarsel` package uses methods to select the most optimal subset of variables that contain cluster information and suggest variables that provide little extra information to drop. It's important to note that these are locally optimal -- depending on where in parameter space the algorithm randomly starts, it is possible that different variables may be selected. 

I chose the most conservative method. The algorithm starts with all the variables, and tests dropping different variables from the equation to see if the difference is minimal (this method is recommended in the clustering textbook I used - will cite).

I tested for a range of 1-5 possible clusters. It's recommended to vary the number of possible clusters between 1 and the next integer after $n^{0.3}$ [4 < 104$^{0.3}$ < 5, @biernacki2006].

From the Resource clusters, the following variables were removed: workers supporting agriculture and hospitality, recreation and developed land, farm size, change in shrublands and land in farms, and median home value.

From the Actors clusters, the following variables were removed: number hired workers.

### Gaussian Model-Based Clustering

To select a model, which includes selecting the number of groups and the shape, I used BIC to test 14 different model shapes and 1-5 possible clusters.

Since this clustering finds local maxima, it is sensitive to its initialization. I ran the cluster models 200 times for each SES subsystem, preserving the best model as the final result.

5 clusters was the best fit for the resource data. 4 clusters was the best fit for the actors data.

The log likelihood values from the bootstrapping process indicate that there are no competing models, so the final models are very likely to be the global as well as local maxima.

```{r}
#| label: "label county data"

clust_dat <- list()

clust_dat[["Resource"]] <- read.csv("data/model results/clust_dat_resource.csv") %>%
  left_join(aoi, by = c("county" = "NAME")) %>%
  st_as_sf()
clust_dat[["Actors"]] <- read.csv("data/model results/clust_dat_actors.csv") %>%
  left_join(aoi, by = c("county" = "NAME")) %>%
  st_as_sf()

resource_means <- clust_dat$Resource %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  pivot_longer(!c(county, year, cluster, GEOID),
               names_to = "input_data_name",
               values_to = "input_data_value") %>%
  group_by(input_data_name) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            min = min(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            max = max(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE))

actor_means <- clust_dat$Actors %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  pivot_longer(!c(county, year, cluster, GEOID),
               names_to = "input_data_name",
               values_to = "input_data_value") %>%
  group_by(input_data_name) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            min = min(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            max = max(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE))
```

#### Cluster R1: Easily developed land with accessible urban and natural amenities

Characteristic resources of R1 are high access to highways and urban areas, higher housing density, more healthcare workers, and flatter land (@fig-R-CIs, @supptblb-data-r1). There is also low presence of federal land and high farm density, characteristics it shares with cluster R5. These counties have experienced higher cropland loss and developed land gain compared to other resource clusters. In general, cluster R1 exhibits wide ranges in its data indicators, showing that counties in this cluster are similar but not homogeneous (@suppfigb-R-ranges, @supptblb-data-r1).

#### Cluster R2: Somewhat isolated counties with forest and mountain amenities

Characteristic resources of R2 are high presence of forestland and more steep lands (@fig-R-CIs). Low land in farms and croplands, low farm density, low access to highways and healthcare, and high federal land are characteristics it shares with R3. These counties are closer to ski areas and have a higher presence of recreation land, and have an average presence of lakes and rivers (@suppfigb-R-ranges, @supptblb-data-r2). There is little urban land, but most of the land in these counties lie within 50 miles of an urban area and its amenities (@supptblb-data-r2). These counties tend to have high home values compared to other clusters (@supptblb-data-r2), indicating the appeal of the natural amenities and non-urban nature of these counties. Despite this appeal, cropland loss and developed land gain are fairly low compared to other clusters.

<!--  Many R2 counties are large (@fig-resource-cluster-map), and data on the large areas of isolated lands can mask the presence and growth of developed areas (e.g. the city of Twin Falls in Twin Falls county). -->

#### Cluster R3: Very isolated counties with few natural amenities

Like R2, R3 has low land in farms and croplands, low farm density, low access to highways and healthcare, and high federal land (@fig-R-CIs). The unique characteristics of R3 are its high shrubland cover and its high distance from urban areas. Natural amenities are also few, with less river miles, fairly low lake area and recreation land, and a high distance to a ski area (@suppfigb-R-ranges). Low cropland cover and larger farms indicate that agriculture in these counties is more focused on livestock grazing (@supptblb-data-r3). R3 has low cropland loss and developed land gain, and it is also losing less farms than other counties (@suppfigb-R-ranges).

#### Cluster R4: Industrial agriculture

R4 has counties with the flattest land and high cropland cover (@fig-R-CIs). Like R2 and R5, there is not much urban land in these counties, but almost all of their lands are within 50 miles of an urban area (@supptblb-data-r4). Access to natural amenities, including lakes, rivers, ski areas, and recreational lands, is low to average for the study area (@suppfigb-R-ranges). Developed land gain is low, but cropland loss, loss of land in farms, and loss of farms themselves is fairly average for the study area (@suppfigb-R-ranges, @supptblb-data-r4).

#### Cluster R5: Rural agriculture as natural amenity

Cluster R5 is characterized by higher land in farms, higher farm density, and more small farms, but also lower presence of croplands and less flat land (@fig-R-CIs, @supptblb-data-r5). Like R2 and R4, these counties do not have much urban land and housing density is low, but most of their lands are within 50 miles of an urban area (@supptblb-data-r5). Though there are many rivers, access to other natural amenities such as ski areas, national parks, lakes, forests, and recreation lands are low (@suppfigb-R-ranges).

#### Cluster A1: High population growth with wealthier, highly educated residents

The defining characteristics of A1 are its high population density and population growth, high incomes, and high percentage of residents with a Bachelor's degree (@fig-A-CIs). A large proportion of jobs are in the tertiary sector -- industries like education, healthcare, hospitality, and other services (@supptblb-data-a1). The county's workforce experiences a mix of urbanicity -- all levels of urbanicity from metropolitan to rural are included in this cluster, and though workers generally live and work in the same county, they also commute to counties with larger urban areas (@supptblb-data-a1). In general, cluster A1 exhibits wide ranges in its data indicators, showing that counties in this cluster are similar but not homogeneous (@suppfigb-A-ranges).

<!-- A1 note: Teton construction jobs going up! -->

#### Cluster A2: More social isolation, less economic opportunity

Cluster A2 is characterized by low population density and the slowest population growth of the study area, the lowest median incomes, and the lower levels of college education (@fig-A-CIs, @suppfigb-A-ranges). These counties have more jobs in the secondary sector (manufacturing, @supptblb-data-a2), and while jobs in agriculture are low, it's important to note that the employment data does not include the self-employed including farmers. Farms in A2 are hiring less workers than the study area average, but less of them are operating at a net loss. A2 counties are all classified as rural, meaning they do not contain an urban area with more than 5,000 residents, indicating a higher level of social isolation. While some of the workforce do commute to counties with urban areas, many live and work in the same rural county (@supptblb-data-a2).

#### Cluster A3: Small cities 

Cluster A3's unique characteristic is that all its counties are micropolitan (contain an urban area with 10,000-49,999 residents, @supptblb-data-a3), and most workers live and work in the same county. A3 is similar to A1 (high population growth with wealthier, highly educated residents), but experiences most indicators to a lesser degree. Population density and growth are at the study area average, and residents have higher incomes and more are college educated, but not at the levels of A1 (@fig-A-CIs). Like A1, many are employed in the tertiary sector, but there are more manufacturing and less construction jobs compared to A1 (@supptblb-data-a3).

#### Cluster A4: Small town counties grow as quickly as small cities

Counties in A4 are "small town" counties (contain an urban area with population 5,000-9,999), have low population density, and are fairly socially isolated with most workers living and working in the same county or another small town county (@fig-A-CIs, @supptblb-data-a4). In many ways, A4 is similar to A2 (more social isolation, less economic opportunity), with less jobs in the tertiary sector, lower incomes, and less people with a Bachelor's degree (@fig-A-CIs). However, the rate of population growth matches that of A3 (small cities) and some A4 counties transition to A3 when their urban areas gain a larger population.

## Cluster Transitions

```{r}
  mutate(cluster = factor(cluster,
                          levels = c("R1", "R2", "R3", "R4", "R5"),
                          labels = c("R1:\nEasily developed land with accessible urban and natural amenties",
                                     "R2:\nSomewhat isolated counties with forest and mountain amenities",
                                     "R3:\nVery isolated counties with few natural amenities",
                                     "R4:\nIndustrial agriculture",
                                     "R5:\nRural agriculture as natural amenity"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(fill = cluster)) +
  geom_sf() +
  # facet_wrap(vars(year)) +
  scale_fill_manual(name = "", values = rev(viridis::turbo(5, begin=0.075, end=0.8)),
                    labels = function(x) str_wrap(x, width = 20, whitespace_only = FALSE)) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position="bottom",
        legend.spacing.x = unit(0, 'cm'))+
  guides(fill = guide_legend(label.position = "bottom",
                             keywidth = 5.5))


actor_map <- clust_dat[["Actors"]] %>%
  mutate(cluster = factor(cluster,
                          levels = c("A1", "A2", "A3", "A4"),
                          labels = c("A1:\nHigh population growth with wealthier, highly educated residents",
                                     "A2:\nMore social isolation, less economic opportunity",
                                     "A3:\nSmall cities",
                                     "A4:\nSmall town counties grow as quickly as small cities"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(fill = cluster)) +
  geom_sf() +
  facet_wrap(vars(year)) +
  scale_fill_manual(name = "", values = rev(viridis::viridis(4)),
                    labels = function(x) str_wrap(x, width = 20, whitespace_only = FALSE)) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position="bottom",
        legend.spacing.x = unit(0, 'cm'))+
  guides(fill = guide_legend(label.position = "bottom",
                             keywidth = 5.5))

resource_map + actor_map + plot_layout(ncol = 1) + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "a")
```

Counties did not transition between resource clusters over the 40 year time period.

A common actor transition was A4 (small towns grow as quickly as small cities) to A3 (small cities), or A2 (more social isolation, less economic opportunity) to A4 (small towns) as population growth fueled the growth of urban areas. One county, Teton, transitioned straight from socially isolated to A1 (high population growth with wealthier, highly educated residents). Elmore County experienced multiple actor transitions (A2 to A1 to A3), and its volatility is likely tied to most of its population being associated with a military base.

## Case Studies

Here I'd like to qualitatively explain how the dynamics of certain counties fit their archetypes. Here are some possibilities:

- Ada/Canyon counties: R1 (easily developed land with accessible urban and natural amenities) and A1 (high population growth with wealthier, highly educated residents) -- classic case of urban sprawl
- Teton County: R1 (easily developed land with accessible urban and natural amenities) and A2 (more social isolation, less economic opportunity) $\rightarrow$ A1 (high population growth with wealthier, highly educated residents) -- "discovery" of natural amenities, inflow of wealthy immigrants
- Blaine County: R2 (somewhat isolated counties with forest and mountain amenities) and A1 (high population growth with wealthier, highly educated residents) -- history of wealth creates "mimicry" of more isolated counties
- Twin Falls County: R4 (industrial agriculture) and A3 (small cities): city built around processing agricultural products, resource cluster indicates that its not as at risk for urban sprawl? (investigate this claim) / its neighbor Jerome County: R1 (easily developed land with accessible urban and natural amenities) and A4 (small town counties grow as quickly as small cities) $\rightarrow$ A3 (small cities) --  flat land that has been used for agriculture at risk of conversion to urban

Some combination of these case studies can tie back to the archetypes I laid out in the intro, but add more information about them.

# Main Takeaways

## Farmlands are threatened by more than urban growth

R1, the cluster losing the most cropland and land in farms and gaining the most developed land, contains both counties that exhibit the traditional patterns of urban sprawl (i.e. Ada and Canyon counties) but also counties that lean more toward patterns of amenity migration (i.e. Teton County). However, these counties also have wide ranges of data indicators, and some aren't losing much farmland or gaining developed land. Once the base resource system of easy-to-develop land becomes desired and A1 actors are attracted, these counties might be most at risk of farmland loss (as seen in Teton). 

Also, transition to A1 can happen anywhere (rural, small town, micropolitan, metropolitan, all types are in A1), so using urbanicity alone might weaken models that try to predict farmland conversion.

## Building block archetypes for the resources and actors of a county as well as its history give us the fuller picture

- Ada and Blaine have the same actors
- Ada and Jerome have the same resource system
- Ada and Teton have the same actors and resource system in 2020

Yet despite sharing similarities, farmland loss and farmland protection is manifested differently in each county. It's important to consider resources, actors, and history when planning for farmland protection. Dynamic archetype analysis (finding archetypes through time) is a useful tool for this. Also, longitudinally comparable datasets are important for this work, but in this analysis, we've laid the blueprint to use public data in this way for any region in the US.

## Archetype analysis links spatially disparate but thematically similar counties

This analysis recontextualizes counties in the study area, allowing us to link counties that are spatially distant but have similar resources and actors. For example, Teton and Ada counties share a resource archetype, and Teton transitioned to the same actor archetype as Ada, alerting us that Teton might soon experience similar levels of urban growth to Ada county.

## Limitations

Some discussion of using counties as a base spatial unit is warranted, especially because some counties are really big. For example, I'd say Twin Falls has traits of R1 and R4 in different locations, but at the county level some of these characteristics are masked.

_C Stock Protection:_ Cluster R2 provides above average C stock protection. This makes sense since R2 is associated with forested, mountainous areas.

_Climate Adaptation:_ Clusters R2 and R4 are areas with more ability to adapt to climate change. These are more likely to have A1 Actor clusters (more educated urbanites). This result points to issues of environmental justice, where more educated (so I'm assuming, more wealthy) actors are also the most well positioned to adapt to climate change. R1 also has A1 actors, but has other actor clusters as well, and this is reflected in the wide spread of climate adaptation NCP.

_Food and Feed:_ Resource clusters with potential for more croplands (R1, R4, R5) provide above average food and feed NCP.

_Habitat:_ The Resource clusters where agriculture and development are limited by rugged conditions (R3, and R2 to a lesser degree) generally provide higher than average habitat NCP. More agricultural (R5) and urban (R4) clusters generally provide less habitat on average, but they have a wide range, indicating that they provide different types of habitat NCP to different levels.

_Recreation:_ Most Resource clusters provide recreation NCP near the average for the study area.

_Water Quality:_ Most Resource clusters are near average here.

# Main Takeaways

## Farmlands are threatened by more than urban growth

The original inspiration for this dissertation chapter was the observation that farmland loss prediction models underestimate farmland loss that isn't associated with urban growth. This analysis, and especially archetype R1, show that the average condition for this study area is farmland loss in places without large urban areas.

## Archetype analysis links spatially disparate but thematically similar counties

This analysis recontextualizes counties in the study area, allowing us to link counties that are spatially distant but have similar resources and actors. For example, though Twin Falls is far from Jefferson, both experience similar types of land use change and have the similar types of actors, and thus may borrow successful farmland protection strategies from each other. 

## Resource systems did not transition, even when actors changed. However, A1 actors in particular can lead to within-cluster shifts

Overall, I found that resource archetypes remained stable over this 40 year period while actor archetypes were more likely to change. This is reasonable for two reasons: (1) populations are more mobile than land systems, so it is easier for them to change, and (2) the difference between land systems (e.g. the dry shrublands of Owyhee and the forested recreation lands of Blaine) is greater than the difference between human populations, so it would require a greater change to shift resource archetypes compared to actor archetypes.

The presence of A1 actors (educated, growing, urban population) is associated with changes in resource systems, even if no counties transitioned from one resource archetype to another. Counties with A1 actors tend to accelerate their developed land growth and housing density. However, A1 does not always mean accelerated development, as evidenced by Blaine County, which has had wealthy inhabitants for a long time and has implemented land protections so that their resource system more closely matches more isolated counties.

## NCP -- ??

I need to think more about the NCP results and if they belong in this chapter. I don't find any surprising results here; the resource systems and their NCP outcomes all seem logical to me. Additionally, the NCP ranges seem to be either really wide or small and all centered on the average (recreation and water quality especially). Both those patterns are difficult to draw conclusions from.

# Appendix A: Data Sources, Processing, and Summary Statistics

## Data Sources and Processing

Code for data retrieval and processing can be found in [notebooks/data_retrieval.qmd](https://github.com/CarolynKoehn/FarmPrES-archetypes/blob/main/notebooks/data_retrieval.qmd). We used the `tidyverse` for data cleaning [v2.0.0, @tidyverse] and the `terra` [v1.7.71, @terra] and `sf` [v1.0.16, @sf] packages for raster and vector data processing, respectively.

Census of Agriculture data was published for 1992, 2002, 2012, and 2022, so data from these years was used to represent agricultural indicators in 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2020. All Census of Agriculture data was downloaded at the county scale.

For all indicators that were simplified to principal components with principal component analysis, we retained principal components that explained >70% of the variance according to @aho2022.

### Resources

#### Percent land in farms

Land in farms and total county land data for 2002-2022 are available in the Census of Agriculture and were retrieved with the USDA NASS API using R package `rnassqs` [v0.6.1, @rnassqs]. Data for 1992 were digitized from the Census of Agriculture Historical Archive, 1992, Idaho, Chapter 2, Table 6 [@CofAg_1992_landinfarms].

#### Percent cropland

Annual land cover data from the National Land Cover Database (NLCD) was downloaded from https://www.mrlc.gov/viewer/ [@nlcd]. We used the `exactextractr` package to summarize the percent cover of each land cover category in each county [v0.10.0, @exactextractr]. To calculate percent cropland, we used the sum of the "Pasture/Hay" and "Cultivated Crops" categories.

#### Percent forestland

Annual land cover data from the National Land Cover Database (NLCD) was downloaded from https://www.mrlc.gov/viewer/ [@nlcd]. We used the `exactextractr` package to summarize the percent cover of each land cover category in each county [v0.10.0, @exactextractr]. To calculate percent forestland, we used the sum of the "Deciduous Forest" and "Evergreen Forest" categories.

#### Percent shrubland

Annual land cover data from the National Land Cover Database (NLCD) was downloaded from https://www.mrlc.gov/viewer/ [@nlcd]. We used the `exactextractr` package to summarize the percent cover of each land cover category in each county [v0.10.0, @exactextractr]. To calculate percent shrubland, we used the "Shrub/Scrub" category.

#### Percent federally managed land

We used the 2023 BLM Idaho Surface Management Agency (Surface Ownership) dataset to represent federal lands [@blm_sma]. We classified the following management agency codes as federal land: BLM, BOR, COE, DOE, DOI, FAA, FHA, GSA, LU_DOI, LU_USDA, MIL, NPS, NWR, USDA, USFS. We then calculated the percent area covered by these management agencies in each county. This indicator was time invariable; federal lands are assumed to not be sold or acquired over the 40 year time period.

#### Lake area

Lake area data is from the Hydrosheds HydroLAKES product [v1.0, @hydrolakes]. We calculated the total area in square kilometers of lakes larger than 10 ha in each county. This indicator is time invariable; we assumed that lake area would not change since 1990.

#### Miles of river

We accessed river data from the WWF HydroSHEDS Free Flowing Rivers Network [v1.0, @hydrosheds] in Google Earth Engine. We filtered to rivers of order 7 or lower which have long-term average discharge >0.1 cubic meters per second. Then, we found the total length of rivers in each county and divided by the county area, so that river length units are in $km/km^2$. This indicator is time invariable; we assumed that river length would not change since 1990.

#### Percent developed land

Annual land cover data from the National Land Cover Database (NLCD) was downloaded from https://www.mrlc.gov/viewer/ [@nlcd]. We used the `exactextractr` package to summarize the percent cover of each land cover category in each county [v0.10.0, @exactextractr]. To calculate percent developed land, we used the sum of the "Developed, Open Space", "Developed, Low Intensity", "Developed, Medium Intensity", and "Developed High Intensity" categories.

#### Land in, nearby, and far from urban areas

Since the definition of urban area changed for the 2020 census, we recreate urban areas for 1990-2020 with the 2020 definitions and thresholds. We first downloaded population size and housing unit count data for census blocks, 1990-2020, within 150 miles of Idaho from IPUMS [@ipums]. Then, we designated any census blocks with housing density $\geq$425 $units/mi^2$ as initial urban core blocks. Then, we added adjacent census blocks with housing density $\geq$200 $units/mi^2$ to the urban cores, repeating this process until there were no census blocks with housing density $\geq$200 $units/mi^2$ adjacent to the urban cores. Finally, we filtered out any urban cores without a high density urban nucleus, defined as a census block with housing density $\geq$1,275 $units/mi^2$, and we filtered out any urban cores with $\leq$2,000 houses or $\leq$5,000 residents. After these urban areas were established, land in each county was classified as "within an urban area," "within 10 mi of an urban area," "within 20 mi of an urban area," increasing in units of 10 mi, with the final category being ">100 mi from an urban area." Then, we calculated the percent cover of each category in each county. This process was repeated for each year, as population growth shifted urban boundaries and created new urban areas. Then, these data were used in a principal component analysis. We retained the first two principal components, which explained 75.8% of the variance.

#### Farm density

Number of farms and total county land data for 2002-2022 are available in the Census of Agriculture and were retrieved with the USDA NASS API using R package `rnassqs` [v0.6.1, @rnassqs]. Data for 1992 were digitized from the Census of Agriculture Historical Archive, 1992, Idaho, Chapter 2, Table 6 [@CofAg_1992_landinfarms].

#### Percent land in recreation areas

We used data from the Protected Areas Database, which "was originally designed to support biodiversity assessments; however, its scope expanded in recent years to include all public and nonprofit held lands and waters" [@pad_us].

The following land designations (column `Des_Tp`) were considered recreation lands to calculate percent recreation land in this analysis: Recreation Management Area, National Monument, National Park, State Recreation Area, State Park, National Recreation Area, National Scenic or Historic Trail. Since sas some state parks were misclassified, these additional local designation (column `Loc_Ds`) terms related to recreation were added as well: State Park, Recreation Reservoir, National Recreation Trail, Recreation Area, National Recreation Area, National Monument, SREC, REC, SP, National Park, and Designated - Recreational. To capture time series data, we filtered data by date established and only included parks established before each time point 1990-2020. Parks without an establishment date were assumed to be established before 1990. We calculated the percent area covered by these recreation lands for each county and year.

#### Distance to nearest national park

We calculated the Euclidean distance from the edge of each county to the edge of the closest national park in the PAD-US data [@pad_us]. This indicator was time invariable, as all nearby national parks were established before 1990.

#### Distance to nearest ski area

We calculated the Euclidean distance from the edge of each county to the edge of the closest ski area in the PAD-US data [@pad_us]. This indicator was time invariable, as all nearby ski resorts were in use before 1990.

#### Housing density

Data for the number of houses in each county for 2000-2020 was downloaded via the Census API using the `tidycensus` package [v1.6.3, @tidycensus]. Data for 1990 were digitized from the 1990 Census of Population and Housing [1990 CPH-2-14, @CofPopHous_1990]. We used total county land from the Census of Agriculture retrieved for 2002-2022 from the USDA NASS API using R package `rnassqs` [v0.6.1, @rnassqs] and digitized for 1992 from the Census of Agriculture Historical Archive, 1992, Idaho, Chapter 2, Table 6 [@CofAg_1992_landinfarms].

```{r}
                        ifelse(dist <= 50, "Within 50", "Over 50"))) %>%
  group_by(county, year, label) %>%
  summarise(urb_cat_perc = sum(perc))
```

Resource summary statistics for all counties.

:::

### Actors

```{r}
#| include: false
#| label: "A data"

a1 <- clust_dat[["Actors"]]

a1_means <- a1 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  pivot_longer(!c(county, year, cluster, GEOID),
               names_to = "input_data_name",
               values_to = "input_data_value") %>%
  group_by(input_data_name) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            median = median(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            min = min(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            max = max(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(var_name_clean = factor(input_data_name,
                                 levels = c("pop_per_acre", "perc_pop_change", "emply_pc1", "emply_pc2", "emply_pc3", "perc_retired", "avg_age", "med_income_in_2020_USD", "unemployment_rate", "High.school", "Bachelors", "races_PC1", "perc_hispanic", "tenure_pc1", "perc_farms_w_net_loss", "num_hired", "ruca_proxy_pc1", "ruca_proxy_pc2"),
                                 labels = c("Population Density", "Population Change", "Employment Sectors (PC1)", "Employment Sectors (PC2)", "Employment Sectors (PC3)", "Retirees", "Average Age", "Median Income", "Unemployment Rate", "Residents with High School Education", "Residents with Bachelor's", "Racial Composition (PC1)", "Hispanic Residents", "Full Owned Farms", "Farms with Net Loss", "Hired Ag Workers", "Urbanicity (PC1)", "Urbanicity (PC2)"))) %>%
  arrange(var_name_clean) %>%
  relocate(var_name_clean, .before = input_data_name) %>%
  select(-input_data_name)

###############
# get employment raw data
emply_a1 <- read.csv("data/clean_data_for_PCA/employment_industries.csv") %>%
  pivot_longer(!c("county", "year"),
               names_to = "industry",
               values_to = "perc_workers")

###############
# racial composition
races_a1 <- read.csv("data/clean_data_for_PCA/races_all.csv") %>%
  pivot_longer(!c("county", "year"),
               names_to = "race",
               values_to = "perc")

###############
# farm tenure
tenure_a1 <- read.csv("data/clean_data_for_PCA/farm_own_perc.csv") %>%
  mutate(county = str_to_title(county),
         year = as.integer(year)-2) %>%
  pivot_longer(!c("county", "year"),
               names_to = "tenure",
               values_to = "perc")

###############
# urbanicity
urb_a1 <- read.csv("data/clean_data_for_PCA/commutes_all.csv") %>%
  pivot_longer(!c("county", "year"),
               names_to = "commut_type",
               values_to = "perc")
```

Summary statistics for all study area counties. A selection of urbanicity statistics are reported (all commute types used by >10% of a county's workforce) as there were very many (25) commute type possibilities in the study area, and means are not reported as they were not representative of the overall data spread.

### R1

```{r}
#| include: false
#| label: "R1 data"

r1 <- clust_dat[["Resource"]] %>%
  filter(cluster == "R1")

r1_means <- r1 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  pivot_longer(!c(county, year, cluster, GEOID),
               names_to = "input_data_name",
               values_to = "input_data_value") %>%
  group_by(input_data_name) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            median = median(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            min = min(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            max = max(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(var_name_clean = factor(input_data_name,
                                 levels = c("land_in_farms", "percent_cropland", "percent_forest", "percent_shrubland", "perc_fed", "lake_area_km2", "rivers_km_per_km2", "urb_dist_pc1", "urb_dist_pc2", "percent_developed", "farms_per_acre", "perc_rec", "dist_to_ski", "dist_to_NP", "housing_units_per_acre", "perc_non_fed_road_area_km2", "healthworkers_per_1000", "perc_farms_change", "Perc_change_land_in_farms", "cropland_change", "forest_change", "shrub_change", "developed_change", "perc_farms_w_net_loss", "ag_support_per_1000", "accom_food_per_1000", "med_home_val_in_2020_USD", "farm_size_pc1", "farm_size_pc2", "avg_slope"),
                                 labels = c("Land in Farms", "Cropland", "Forest", "Shrubland", "Federal Land", "Lake Area", "Length of Rivers", "Distance from Urban (PC1)", "Distance from Urban (PC2)","Developed Land", "Farm Density", "Recreation Land", "Distance to a Ski Area", "Distance to a National Park", "Housing Density", "Non-Federal Land near Highway", "Healthcare Workers", "Farm Loss/Gain", "Land in Farms Loss/Gain", "Cropland Loss/Gain", "Forest Loss/Gain", "Shrubland Loss/Gain", "Developed Land Gain", "Farms with Net Loss", "Jobs Supporting Ag", "Jobs in Hospitality", "Med Home Value", "Farm Size (PC1)", "Farm Size (PC2)", "Average Slope"))) %>%
  arrange(var_name_clean) %>%
  relocate(var_name_clean, .before = input_data_name) %>%
  select(-input_data_name)

###############
# get farm size raw data
# farm sizes range
# list parameters
params <- list(state_alpha = "ID",
               agg_level_desc = "county",
               year = c(2002, 2012, 2022),
               commodity_desc = "Farm operations",
               short_desc = "Farm operations - number of operations",
               domain_desc = "area operated")
# retrieve
farm_sizes <- nassqs(params)
# save a backup copy
# write.csv(farm_sizes,
#           "../data/API_data_download_backup/farm_sizes.csv",
#           row.names = FALSE)

# clean
farm_sizes2 <- farm_sizes %>%
  # remove redundant categories
  filter(!(domaincat_desc %in% c("AREA OPERATED: (180 TO 219 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (220 TO 259 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (260 TO 499 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (50.0 TO 69.9 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (70.0 TO 99.9 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (100 TO 139 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (140 TO 179 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (1,000 OR MORE ACRES)"))) %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = c(county_name, year),
              names_from = domaincat_desc,
              values_from = Value) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(total_farms = sum(c_across(`AREA OPERATED: (1,000 TO 1,999 ACRES)`:`AREA OPERATED: (500 TO 999 ACRES)`), na.rm=TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(across(`AREA OPERATED: (1,000 TO 1,999 ACRES)`:`AREA OPERATED: (500 TO 999 ACRES)`,
                ~.x/total_farms*100))

# 1992 data
farm_sizes_1992 <- read.csv("data/Farm_size_1925-1992.csv") %>%
  filter(Year == 1992) %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = c("County", "Year"),
              names_from = "Size",
              values_from = "Num_farms") %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(across(`under 10 acres`:`over 2,000 acres`,
                ~.x/`all farms`*100)) %>%
  # create comparable categories
  mutate(`AREA OPERATED: (1,000 TO 1,999 ACRES)` = `1,000 to 1,999 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (1.0 TO 9.9 ACRES)` = `under 10 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (10.0 TO 49.9 ACRES)` = `10 to 49 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (180 TO 499 ACRES)` = `180 to 219 acres` + `220 to 259 acres` + `260 to 499 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (2,000 OR MORE ACRES)` = `over 2,000 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (50 TO 179 ACRES)` = `50 to 69 acres` + `70 to 99 acres` + `100 to 139 acres` + `140 to 179 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (500 TO 999 ACRES)` = `500 to 999 acres`) %>%
  rename("county_name" = "County",
         "year" = "Year")

# join
farm_sizes_all <- rbind(farm_sizes2[,1:9],
                        farm_sizes_1992[,c(1:2,16:22)]) %>%
  replace(is.na(.), 0) %>%
  mutate(county = str_to_title(county_name),
         year = as.integer(year)-2)

farm_sizes_r1 <- left_join(r1, farm_sizes_all, by = c("county", "year")) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(small_farm_perc = sum(`AREA OPERATED: (1.0 TO 9.9 ACRES)`,
                               `AREA OPERATED: (10.0 TO 49.9 ACRES)`),
         med_farm_perc = sum(`AREA OPERATED: (50 TO 179 ACRES)`,
                             `AREA OPERATED: (180 TO 499 ACRES)`),
         large_farm_perc = sum(`AREA OPERATED: (1,000 TO 1,999 ACRES)`,
                               `AREA OPERATED: (2,000 OR MORE ACRES)`,
                             `AREA OPERATED: (500 TO 999 ACRES)`))

###############
# urb areas
urb_dist_areas_r1 <- read.csv("data/clean_data_for_PCA/urb_dist_areas.csv") %>%
  pivot_longer(!c("county", "year"),
               names_to = "dist",
               values_to = "perc") %>%
  mutate(dist = as.integer(str_extract_all(dist, "\\d+"))) %>%
  filter(county %in% r1$county) %>%
  mutate(label = ifelse(dist == 0, "Urban",
                        ifelse(dist <= 50, "Within 50", "Over 50"))) %>%
  group_by(county, year, label) %>%
  summarise(urb_cat_perc = sum(perc))
```

The counties in R1 are `r names(table(r1$county)[table(r1$county)==4])`.

:::

### R2

```{r}
#| include: false
#| label: "R2 data"

r2 <- clust_dat[["Resource"]] %>%
  filter(cluster == "R2")

r2_means <- r2 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  pivot_longer(!c(county, year, cluster, GEOID),
               names_to = "input_data_name",
               values_to = "input_data_value") %>%
  group_by(input_data_name) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            median = median(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            min = min(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            max = max(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(var_name_clean = factor(input_data_name,
                                 levels = c("land_in_farms", "percent_cropland", "percent_forest", "percent_shrubland", "perc_fed", "lake_area_km2", "rivers_km_per_km2", "urb_dist_pc1", "urb_dist_pc2", "percent_developed", "farms_per_acre", "perc_rec", "dist_to_ski", "dist_to_NP", "housing_units_per_acre", "perc_non_fed_road_area_km2", "healthworkers_per_1000", "perc_farms_change", "Perc_change_land_in_farms", "cropland_change", "forest_change", "shrub_change", "developed_change", "perc_farms_w_net_loss", "ag_support_per_1000", "accom_food_per_1000", "med_home_val_in_2020_USD", "farm_size_pc1", "farm_size_pc2", "avg_slope"),
                                 labels = c("Land in Farms", "Cropland", "Forest", "Shrubland", "Federal Land", "Lake Area", "Length of Rivers", "Distance from Urban (PC1)", "Distance from Urban (PC2)","Developed Land", "Farm Density", "Recreation Land", "Distance to a Ski Area", "Distance to a National Park", "Housing Density", "Non-Federal Land near Highway", "Healthcare Workers", "Farm Loss/Gain", "Land in Farms Loss/Gain", "Cropland Loss/Gain", "Forest Loss/Gain", "Shrubland Loss/Gain", "Developed Land Gain", "Farms with Net Loss", "Jobs Supporting Ag", "Jobs in Hospitality", "Med Home Value", "Farm Size (PC1)", "Farm Size (PC2)", "Average Slope"))) %>%
  arrange(var_name_clean) %>%
  relocate(var_name_clean, .before = input_data_name) %>%
  select(-input_data_name)

###############
# get farm size raw data
# farm sizes range
# list parameters
params <- list(state_alpha = "ID",
               agg_level_desc = "county",
               year = c(2002, 2012, 2022),
               commodity_desc = "Farm operations",
               short_desc = "Farm operations - number of operations",
               domain_desc = "area operated")
# retrieve
farm_sizes <- nassqs(params)
# save a backup copy
# write.csv(farm_sizes,
#           "../data/API_data_download_backup/farm_sizes.csv",
#           row.names = FALSE)

# clean
farm_sizes2 <- farm_sizes %>%
  # remove redundant categories
  filter(!(domaincat_desc %in% c("AREA OPERATED: (180 TO 219 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (220 TO 259 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (260 TO 499 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (50.0 TO 69.9 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (70.0 TO 99.9 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (100 TO 139 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (140 TO 179 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (1,000 OR MORE ACRES)"))) %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = c(county_name, year),
              names_from = domaincat_desc,
              values_from = Value) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(total_farms = sum(c_across(`AREA OPERATED: (1,000 TO 1,999 ACRES)`:`AREA OPERATED: (500 TO 999 ACRES)`), na.rm=TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(across(`AREA OPERATED: (1,000 TO 1,999 ACRES)`:`AREA OPERATED: (500 TO 999 ACRES)`,
                ~.x/total_farms*100))

# 1992 data
farm_sizes_1992 <- read.csv("data/Farm_size_1925-1992.csv") %>%
  filter(Year == 1992) %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = c("County", "Year"),
              names_from = "Size",
              values_from = "Num_farms") %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(across(`under 10 acres`:`over 2,000 acres`,
                ~.x/`all farms`*100)) %>%
  # create comparable categories
  mutate(`AREA OPERATED: (1,000 TO 1,999 ACRES)` = `1,000 to 1,999 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (1.0 TO 9.9 ACRES)` = `under 10 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (10.0 TO 49.9 ACRES)` = `10 to 49 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (180 TO 499 ACRES)` = `180 to 219 acres` + `220 to 259 acres` + `260 to 499 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (2,000 OR MORE ACRES)` = `over 2,000 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (50 TO 179 ACRES)` = `50 to 69 acres` + `70 to 99 acres` + `100 to 139 acres` + `140 to 179 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (500 TO 999 ACRES)` = `500 to 999 acres`) %>%
  rename("county_name" = "County",
         "year" = "Year")

# join
farm_sizes_all <- rbind(farm_sizes2[,1:9],
                        farm_sizes_1992[,c(1:2,16:22)]) %>%
  replace(is.na(.), 0) %>%
  mutate(county = str_to_title(county_name),
         year = as.integer(year)-2)

farm_sizes_r2 <- left_join(r2, farm_sizes_all, by = c("county", "year")) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(small_farm_perc = sum(`AREA OPERATED: (1.0 TO 9.9 ACRES)`,
                               `AREA OPERATED: (10.0 TO 49.9 ACRES)`),
         med_farm_perc = sum(`AREA OPERATED: (50 TO 179 ACRES)`,
                             `AREA OPERATED: (180 TO 499 ACRES)`),
         large_farm_perc = sum(`AREA OPERATED: (1,000 TO 1,999 ACRES)`,
                               `AREA OPERATED: (2,000 OR MORE ACRES)`,
                             `AREA OPERATED: (500 TO 999 ACRES)`))

###############
# urb areas
urb_dist_areas_r2 <- read.csv("data/clean_data_for_PCA/urb_dist_areas.csv") %>%
  pivot_longer(!c("county", "year"),
               names_to = "dist",
               values_to = "perc") %>%
  mutate(dist = as.integer(str_extract_all(dist, "\\d+"))) %>%
  filter(county %in% r2$county) %>%
  mutate(label = ifelse(dist == 0, "Urban",
                        ifelse(dist <= 50, "Within 50", "Over 50"))) %>%
  group_by(county, year, label) %>%
  summarise(urb_cat_perc = sum(perc))
```

The counties in R2 are `r names(table(r2$county)[table(r2$county)==4])`.

:::

### R3

```{r}
#| include: false
#| label: "R3 data"

r3 <- clust_dat[["Resource"]] %>%
  filter(cluster == "R3")

r3_means <- r3 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  pivot_longer(!c(county, year, cluster, GEOID),
               names_to = "input_data_name",
               values_to = "input_data_value") %>%
  group_by(input_data_name) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            median = median(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            min = min(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            max = max(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(var_name_clean = factor(input_data_name,
                                 levels = c("land_in_farms", "percent_cropland", "percent_forest", "percent_shrubland", "perc_fed", "lake_area_km2", "rivers_km_per_km2", "urb_dist_pc1", "urb_dist_pc2", "percent_developed", "farms_per_acre", "perc_rec", "dist_to_ski", "dist_to_NP", "housing_units_per_acre", "perc_non_fed_road_area_km2", "healthworkers_per_1000", "perc_farms_change", "Perc_change_land_in_farms", "cropland_change", "forest_change", "shrub_change", "developed_change", "perc_farms_w_net_loss", "ag_support_per_1000", "accom_food_per_1000", "med_home_val_in_2020_USD", "farm_size_pc1", "farm_size_pc2", "avg_slope"),
                                 labels = c("Land in Farms", "Cropland", "Forest", "Shrubland", "Federal Land", "Lake Area", "Length of Rivers", "Distance from Urban (PC1)", "Distance from Urban (PC2)","Developed Land", "Farm Density", "Recreation Land", "Distance to a Ski Area", "Distance to a National Park", "Housing Density", "Non-Federal Land near Highway", "Healthcare Workers", "Farm Loss/Gain", "Land in Farms Loss/Gain", "Cropland Loss/Gain", "Forest Loss/Gain", "Shrubland Loss/Gain", "Developed Land Gain", "Farms with Net Loss", "Jobs Supporting Ag", "Jobs in Hospitality", "Med Home Value", "Farm Size (PC1)", "Farm Size (PC2)", "Average Slope"))) %>%
  arrange(var_name_clean) %>%
  relocate(var_name_clean, .before = input_data_name) %>%
  select(-input_data_name)

###############
# get farm size raw data
# farm sizes range
# list parameters
params <- list(state_alpha = "ID",
               agg_level_desc = "county",
               year = c(2002, 2012, 2022),
               commodity_desc = "Farm operations",
               short_desc = "Farm operations - number of operations",
               domain_desc = "area operated")
# retrieve
farm_sizes <- nassqs(params)
# save a backup copy
# write.csv(farm_sizes,
#           "../data/API_data_download_backup/farm_sizes.csv",
#           row.names = FALSE)

# clean
farm_sizes2 <- farm_sizes %>%
  # remove redundant categories
  filter(!(domaincat_desc %in% c("AREA OPERATED: (180 TO 219 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (220 TO 259 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (260 TO 499 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (50.0 TO 69.9 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (70.0 TO 99.9 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (100 TO 139 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (140 TO 179 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (1,000 OR MORE ACRES)"))) %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = c(county_name, year),
              names_from = domaincat_desc,
              values_from = Value) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(total_farms = sum(c_across(`AREA OPERATED: (1,000 TO 1,999 ACRES)`:`AREA OPERATED: (500 TO 999 ACRES)`), na.rm=TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(across(`AREA OPERATED: (1,000 TO 1,999 ACRES)`:`AREA OPERATED: (500 TO 999 ACRES)`,
                ~.x/total_farms*100))

# 1992 data
farm_sizes_1992 <- read.csv("data/Farm_size_1925-1992.csv") %>%
  filter(Year == 1992) %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = c("County", "Year"),
              names_from = "Size",
              values_from = "Num_farms") %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(across(`under 10 acres`:`over 2,000 acres`,
                ~.x/`all farms`*100)) %>%
  # create comparable categories
  mutate(`AREA OPERATED: (1,000 TO 1,999 ACRES)` = `1,000 to 1,999 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (1.0 TO 9.9 ACRES)` = `under 10 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (10.0 TO 49.9 ACRES)` = `10 to 49 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (180 TO 499 ACRES)` = `180 to 219 acres` + `220 to 259 acres` + `260 to 499 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (2,000 OR MORE ACRES)` = `over 2,000 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (50 TO 179 ACRES)` = `50 to 69 acres` + `70 to 99 acres` + `100 to 139 acres` + `140 to 179 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (500 TO 999 ACRES)` = `500 to 999 acres`) %>%
  rename("county_name" = "County",
         "year" = "Year")

# join
farm_sizes_all <- rbind(farm_sizes2[,1:9],
                        farm_sizes_1992[,c(1:2,16:22)]) %>%
  replace(is.na(.), 0) %>%
  mutate(county = str_to_title(county_name),
         year = as.integer(year)-2)

farm_sizes_r3 <- left_join(r3, farm_sizes_all, by = c("county", "year")) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(small_farm_perc = sum(`AREA OPERATED: (1.0 TO 9.9 ACRES)`,
                               `AREA OPERATED: (10.0 TO 49.9 ACRES)`),
         med_farm_perc = sum(`AREA OPERATED: (50 TO 179 ACRES)`,
                             `AREA OPERATED: (180 TO 499 ACRES)`),
         large_farm_perc = sum(`AREA OPERATED: (1,000 TO 1,999 ACRES)`,
                               `AREA OPERATED: (2,000 OR MORE ACRES)`,
                             `AREA OPERATED: (500 TO 999 ACRES)`))

###############
# urb areas
urb_dist_areas_r3 <- read.csv("data/clean_data_for_PCA/urb_dist_areas.csv") %>%
  pivot_longer(!c("county", "year"),
               names_to = "dist",
               values_to = "perc") %>%
  mutate(dist = as.integer(str_extract_all(dist, "\\d+"))) %>%
  filter(county %in% r3$county) %>%
  mutate(label = ifelse(dist == 0, "Urban",
                        ifelse(dist <= 50, "Within 50", "Over 50"))) %>%
  group_by(county, year, label) %>%
  summarise(urb_cat_perc = sum(perc))
```

The counties in R3 are `r names(table(r3$county)[table(r3$county)==4])`.

### R4

```{r}
#| include: false
#| label: "R4 data"

r4 <- clust_dat[["Resource"]] %>%
  filter(cluster == "R4")

r4_means <- r4 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  pivot_longer(!c(county, year, cluster, GEOID),
               names_to = "input_data_name",
               values_to = "input_data_value") %>%
  group_by(input_data_name) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            median = median(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            min = min(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            max = max(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(var_name_clean = factor(input_data_name,
                                 levels = c("land_in_farms", "percent_cropland", "percent_forest", "percent_shrubland", "perc_fed", "lake_area_km2", "rivers_km_per_km2", "urb_dist_pc1", "urb_dist_pc2", "percent_developed", "farms_per_acre", "perc_rec", "dist_to_ski", "dist_to_NP", "housing_units_per_acre", "perc_non_fed_road_area_km2", "healthworkers_per_1000", "perc_farms_change", "Perc_change_land_in_farms", "cropland_change", "forest_change", "shrub_change", "developed_change", "perc_farms_w_net_loss", "ag_support_per_1000", "accom_food_per_1000", "med_home_val_in_2020_USD", "farm_size_pc1", "farm_size_pc2", "avg_slope"),
                                 labels = c("Land in Farms", "Cropland", "Forest", "Shrubland", "Federal Land", "Lake Area", "Length of Rivers", "Distance from Urban (PC1)", "Distance from Urban (PC2)","Developed Land", "Farm Density", "Recreation Land", "Distance to a Ski Area", "Distance to a National Park", "Housing Density", "Non-Federal Land near Highway", "Healthcare Workers", "Farm Loss/Gain", "Land in Farms Loss/Gain", "Cropland Loss/Gain", "Forest Loss/Gain", "Shrubland Loss/Gain", "Developed Land Gain", "Farms with Net Loss", "Jobs Supporting Ag", "Jobs in Hospitality", "Med Home Value", "Farm Size (PC1)", "Farm Size (PC2)", "Average Slope"))) %>%
  arrange(var_name_clean) %>%
  relocate(var_name_clean, .before = input_data_name) %>%
  select(-input_data_name)

###############
# get farm size raw data
# farm sizes range
# list parameters
params <- list(state_alpha = "ID",
               agg_level_desc = "county",
               year = c(2002, 2012, 2022),
               commodity_desc = "Farm operations",
               short_desc = "Farm operations - number of operations",
               domain_desc = "area operated")
# retrieve
farm_sizes <- nassqs(params)
# save a backup copy
# write.csv(farm_sizes,
#           "../data/API_data_download_backup/farm_sizes.csv",
#           row.names = FALSE)

# clean
farm_sizes2 <- farm_sizes %>%
  # remove redundant categories
  filter(!(domaincat_desc %in% c("AREA OPERATED: (180 TO 219 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (220 TO 259 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (260 TO 499 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (50.0 TO 69.9 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (70.0 TO 99.9 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (100 TO 139 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (140 TO 179 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (1,000 OR MORE ACRES)"))) %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = c(county_name, year),
              names_from = domaincat_desc,
              values_from = Value) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(total_farms = sum(c_across(`AREA OPERATED: (1,000 TO 1,999 ACRES)`:`AREA OPERATED: (500 TO 999 ACRES)`), na.rm=TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(across(`AREA OPERATED: (1,000 TO 1,999 ACRES)`:`AREA OPERATED: (500 TO 999 ACRES)`,
                ~.x/total_farms*100))

# 1992 data
farm_sizes_1992 <- read.csv("data/Farm_size_1925-1992.csv") %>%
  filter(Year == 1992) %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = c("County", "Year"),
              names_from = "Size",
              values_from = "Num_farms") %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(across(`under 10 acres`:`over 2,000 acres`,
                ~.x/`all farms`*100)) %>%
  # create comparable categories
  mutate(`AREA OPERATED: (1,000 TO 1,999 ACRES)` = `1,000 to 1,999 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (1.0 TO 9.9 ACRES)` = `under 10 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (10.0 TO 49.9 ACRES)` = `10 to 49 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (180 TO 499 ACRES)` = `180 to 219 acres` + `220 to 259 acres` + `260 to 499 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (2,000 OR MORE ACRES)` = `over 2,000 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (50 TO 179 ACRES)` = `50 to 69 acres` + `70 to 99 acres` + `100 to 139 acres` + `140 to 179 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (500 TO 999 ACRES)` = `500 to 999 acres`) %>%
  rename("county_name" = "County",
         "year" = "Year")

# join
farm_sizes_all <- rbind(farm_sizes2[,1:9],
                        farm_sizes_1992[,c(1:2,16:22)]) %>%
  replace(is.na(.), 0) %>%
  mutate(county = str_to_title(county_name),
         year = as.integer(year)-2)

farm_sizes_r4 <- left_join(r4, farm_sizes_all, by = c("county", "year")) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(small_farm_perc = sum(`AREA OPERATED: (1.0 TO 9.9 ACRES)`,
                               `AREA OPERATED: (10.0 TO 49.9 ACRES)`),
         med_farm_perc = sum(`AREA OPERATED: (50 TO 179 ACRES)`,
                             `AREA OPERATED: (180 TO 499 ACRES)`),
         large_farm_perc = sum(`AREA OPERATED: (1,000 TO 1,999 ACRES)`,
                               `AREA OPERATED: (2,000 OR MORE ACRES)`,
                             `AREA OPERATED: (500 TO 999 ACRES)`))

###############
# urb areas
urb_dist_areas_r4 <- read.csv("data/clean_data_for_PCA/urb_dist_areas.csv") %>%
  pivot_longer(!c("county", "year"),
               names_to = "dist",
               values_to = "perc") %>%
  mutate(dist = as.integer(str_extract_all(dist, "\\d+"))) %>%
  filter(county %in% r4$county) %>%
  mutate(label = ifelse(dist == 0, "Urban",
                        ifelse(dist <= 50, "Within 50", "Over 50"))) %>%
  group_by(county, year, label) %>%
  summarise(urb_cat_perc = sum(perc))
```

The counties in R4 are `r names(table(r4$county)[table(r4$county)==4])`.

### R5

```{r}
#| include: false
#| label: "R5 data"

r5 <- clust_dat[["Resource"]] %>%
  filter(cluster == "R5")

r5_means <- r5 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  pivot_longer(!c(county, year, cluster, GEOID),
               names_to = "input_data_name",
               values_to = "input_data_value") %>%
  group_by(input_data_name) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            median = median(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            min = min(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            max = max(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(var_name_clean = factor(input_data_name,
                                 levels = c("land_in_farms", "percent_cropland", "percent_forest", "percent_shrubland", "perc_fed", "lake_area_km2", "rivers_km_per_km2", "urb_dist_pc1", "urb_dist_pc2", "percent_developed", "farms_per_acre", "perc_rec", "dist_to_ski", "dist_to_NP", "housing_units_per_acre", "perc_non_fed_road_area_km2", "healthworkers_per_1000", "perc_farms_change", "Perc_change_land_in_farms", "cropland_change", "forest_change", "shrub_change", "developed_change", "perc_farms_w_net_loss", "ag_support_per_1000", "accom_food_per_1000", "med_home_val_in_2020_USD", "farm_size_pc1", "farm_size_pc2", "avg_slope"),
                                 labels = c("Land in Farms", "Cropland", "Forest", "Shrubland", "Federal Land", "Lake Area", "Length of Rivers", "Distance from Urban (PC1)", "Distance from Urban (PC2)","Developed Land", "Farm Density", "Recreation Land", "Distance to a Ski Area", "Distance to a National Park", "Housing Density", "Non-Federal Land near Highway", "Healthcare Workers", "Farm Loss/Gain", "Land in Farms Loss/Gain", "Cropland Loss/Gain", "Forest Loss/Gain", "Shrubland Loss/Gain", "Developed Land Gain", "Farms with Net Loss", "Jobs Supporting Ag", "Jobs in Hospitality", "Med Home Value", "Farm Size (PC1)", "Farm Size (PC2)", "Average Slope"))) %>%
  arrange(var_name_clean) %>%
  relocate(var_name_clean, .before = input_data_name) %>%
  select(-input_data_name)

###############
# get farm size raw data
# farm sizes range
# list parameters
params <- list(state_alpha = "ID",
               agg_level_desc = "county",
               year = c(2002, 2012, 2022),
               commodity_desc = "Farm operations",
               short_desc = "Farm operations - number of operations",
               domain_desc = "area operated")
# retrieve
farm_sizes <- nassqs(params)
# save a backup copy
# write.csv(farm_sizes,
#           "../data/API_data_download_backup/farm_sizes.csv",
#           row.names = FALSE)

# clean
farm_sizes2 <- farm_sizes %>%
  # remove redundant categories
  filter(!(domaincat_desc %in% c("AREA OPERATED: (180 TO 219 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (220 TO 259 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (260 TO 499 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (50.0 TO 69.9 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (70.0 TO 99.9 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (100 TO 139 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (140 TO 179 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (1,000 OR MORE ACRES)"))) %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = c(county_name, year),
              names_from = domaincat_desc,
              values_from = Value) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(total_farms = sum(c_across(`AREA OPERATED: (1,000 TO 1,999 ACRES)`:`AREA OPERATED: (500 TO 999 ACRES)`), na.rm=TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(across(`AREA OPERATED: (1,000 TO 1,999 ACRES)`:`AREA OPERATED: (500 TO 999 ACRES)`,
                ~.x/total_farms*100))

# 1992 data
farm_sizes_1992 <- read.csv("data/Farm_size_1925-1992.csv") %>%
  filter(Year == 1992) %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = c("County", "Year"),
              names_from = "Size",
              values_from = "Num_farms") %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(across(`under 10 acres`:`over 2,000 acres`,
                ~.x/`all farms`*100)) %>%
  # create comparable categories
  mutate(`AREA OPERATED: (1,000 TO 1,999 ACRES)` = `1,000 to 1,999 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (1.0 TO 9.9 ACRES)` = `under 10 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (10.0 TO 49.9 ACRES)` = `10 to 49 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (180 TO 499 ACRES)` = `180 to 219 acres` + `220 to 259 acres` + `260 to 499 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (2,000 OR MORE ACRES)` = `over 2,000 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (50 TO 179 ACRES)` = `50 to 69 acres` + `70 to 99 acres` + `100 to 139 acres` + `140 to 179 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (500 TO 999 ACRES)` = `500 to 999 acres`) %>%
  rename("county_name" = "County",
         "year" = "Year")

# join
farm_sizes_all <- rbind(farm_sizes2[,1:9],
                        farm_sizes_1992[,c(1:2,16:22)]) %>%
  replace(is.na(.), 0) %>%
  mutate(county = str_to_title(county_name),
         year = as.integer(year)-2)

farm_sizes_r5 <- left_join(r5, farm_sizes_all, by = c("county", "year")) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(small_farm_perc = sum(`AREA OPERATED: (1.0 TO 9.9 ACRES)`,
                               `AREA OPERATED: (10.0 TO 49.9 ACRES)`),
         med_farm_perc = sum(`AREA OPERATED: (50 TO 179 ACRES)`,
                             `AREA OPERATED: (180 TO 499 ACRES)`),
         large_farm_perc = sum(`AREA OPERATED: (1,000 TO 1,999 ACRES)`,
                               `AREA OPERATED: (2,000 OR MORE ACRES)`,
                             `AREA OPERATED: (500 TO 999 ACRES)`))

###############
# urb areas
urb_dist_areas_r5 <- read.csv("data/clean_data_for_PCA/urb_dist_areas.csv") %>%
  pivot_longer(!c("county", "year"),
               names_to = "dist",
               values_to = "perc") %>%
  mutate(dist = as.integer(str_extract_all(dist, "\\d+"))) %>%
  filter(county %in% r5$county) %>%
  mutate(label = ifelse(dist == 0, "Urban",
                        ifelse(dist <= 50, "Within 50", "Over 50"))) %>%
  group_by(county, year, label) %>%
  summarise(urb_cat_perc = sum(perc))
```

The counties in R5 are `r names(table(r5$county)[table(r5$county)==4])`.

```{r}
#| message: false

clust_dat_sc[["Actors"]] %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = !c(county, year, cluster, GEOID),
               names_to = "input_data_name",
               values_to = "value") %>%
  left_join(ci_clust[["Actors"]][,c("cluster", "input_data_name", "sig")]) %>%
  mutate(sig = ifelse(is.na(sig), "Not in model", sig)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value, y = input_data_name, fill = sig, alpha = sig, color=sig)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept=0, color = "black", linetype="dashed") +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-1,1)) +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev(c("pop_per_acre", "perc_pop_change", "emply_pc1", "emply_pc2", "emply_pc3", "perc_retired", "avg_age", "med_income_in_2020_USD", "unemployment_rate", "High.school", "Bachelors", "races_PC1", "perc_hispanic", "tenure_pc1", "perc_farms_w_net_loss", "num_hired", "ruca_proxy_pc1", "ruca_proxy_pc2")),
                   labels = rev(c("Population Density", "Population Change", "Employment Sectors (PC1)", "Employment Sectors (PC2)", "Employment Sectors (PC3)", "Retirees", "Average Age", "Median Income", "Unemployment Rate", "Residents with High School Education", "Residents with Bachelor's", "Racial Composition (PC1)", "Hispanic Residents", "Full Owned Farms", "Farms with Net Loss", "Hired Ag Workers", "Urbanicity (PC1)", "Urbanicity (PC2)"))) +
  scale_fill_manual(limits = c("TRUE", "FALSE", "Not in model"),
                    values = c("orchid3", "orchid3", "beige"),
                    labels = c("Yes", "No", "Not in model\n(removed during\nvariable selection)"),
                    name = "Cluster mean\nsignificantly different\nfrom study area mean\n(p<0.05)") +
  scale_alpha_manual(limits = c("TRUE", "FALSE", "Not in model"),
                    values = c(1, 0.3, 0.3),
                    labels = c("Yes", "No", "Not in model\n(removed during\nvariable selection)"), 
                    name = "Cluster mean\nsignificantly different\nfrom study area mean\n(p<0.05)") +
  scale_color_manual(limits = c("TRUE", "FALSE", "Not in model"),
                    values = c("black", "gray50", "gray50"),
                    labels = c("Yes", "No", "Not in model\n(removed during\nvariable selection)"),
                    name = "Cluster mean\nsignificantly different\nfrom study area mean\n(p<0.05)") +
  facet_wrap(vars(cluster)) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

### A1

```{r}
#| include: false
#| label: "A1 data"

a1 <- clust_dat[["Actors"]] %>%
  filter(cluster == "A1")

a1_means <- a1 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  pivot_longer(!c(county, year, cluster, GEOID),
               names_to = "input_data_name",
               values_to = "input_data_value") %>%
  group_by(input_data_name) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            median = median(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            min = min(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            max = max(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(var_name_clean = factor(input_data_name,
                                 levels = c("pop_per_acre", "perc_pop_change", "emply_pc1", "emply_pc2", "emply_pc3", "perc_retired", "avg_age", "med_income_in_2020_USD", "unemployment_rate", "High.school", "Bachelors", "races_PC1", "perc_hispanic", "tenure_pc1", "perc_farms_w_net_loss", "num_hired", "ruca_proxy_pc1", "ruca_proxy_pc2"),
                                 labels = c("Population Density", "Population Change", "Employment Sectors (PC1)", "Employment Sectors (PC2)", "Employment Sectors (PC3)", "Retirees", "Average Age", "Median Income", "Unemployment Rate", "Residents with High School Education", "Residents with Bachelor's", "Racial Composition (PC1)", "Hispanic Residents", "Full Owned Farms", "Farms with Net Loss", "Hired Ag Workers", "Urbanicity (PC1)", "Urbanicity (PC2)"))) %>%
  arrange(var_name_clean) %>%
  relocate(var_name_clean, .before = input_data_name) %>%
  select(-input_data_name)

###############
# get employment raw data
emply_a1 <- read.csv("data/clean_data_for_PCA/employment_industries.csv") %>%
  right_join(st_drop_geometry(a1[,c(1:2)])) %>%
  pivot_longer(!c("county", "year"),
               names_to = "industry",
               values_to = "perc_workers")

###############
# racial composition
races_a1 <- read.csv("data/clean_data_for_PCA/races_all.csv") %>%
  right_join(st_drop_geometry(a1[,c(1:2)])) %>%
  pivot_longer(!c("county", "year"),
               names_to = "race",
               values_to = "perc")

###############
# farm tenure
tenure_a1 <- read.csv("data/clean_data_for_PCA/farm_own_perc.csv") %>%
  mutate(county = str_to_title(county),
         year = as.integer(year)-2) %>%
  right_join(st_drop_geometry(a1[,c(1:2)])) %>%
  pivot_longer(!c("county", "year"),
               names_to = "tenure",
               values_to = "perc")

###############
# urbanicity
urb_a1 <- read.csv("data/clean_data_for_PCA/commutes_all.csv") %>%
  right_join(st_drop_geometry(a1[,c(1:2)])) %>%
  pivot_longer(!c("county", "year"),
               names_to = "commut_type",
               values_to = "perc")
```

The counties in A1 are Ada, Blaine, Canyon, Madison, Teton (2000-2020), and Elmore (2000).
